model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does enabling Inner Monologue affect Moshi's spoken question answering accuracy across Web Questions, LlaMA-Questions, and Audio TriviaQA, and how can the same architecture be switched into streaming ASR or streaming TTS without changing the loss or architecture?
reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. The same multi‑stream architecture can be repurposed for streaming ASR or streaming TTS simply by adjusting the delay between text and audio tokens—no change to the loss function or the underlying model is required—because Inner Monologue’s prefix‑generation framework is compatible with any streaming inference setup [moshi-C-077].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation. model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How do the three papers address sequence length scaling and computational bottlenecks in autoregressive or transduction modeling?
reply: The Moshi v1 paper tackles sequence‑length scaling by introducing a *hierarchical* autoregressive model—the RQ‑Transformer—where a large Temporal Transformer first processes long‑time‑step sequences to produce a context vector, and a smaller Depth Transformer then predicts the tokens within each time step. This two‑stage design allows the model to scale to longer sequences simply by increasing the number of time steps \(S\), while keeping the per‑step depth \(K\) small, thereby reducing the overall computational burden per prediction step [moshi-C-023][moshi-C-021].[Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]

question: In H-Net, how does the routing module compute boundary probabilities $p_t$ and discrete boundary indicators $b_t$, and what is the formula and weight $\alpha$ for the auxiliary ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}$?

In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

model_record.content:
The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]  

The auxiliary ratio loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}\) is defined to enforce that the ratio of retained tokens matches a target ratio, but its explicit formula and the weighting coefficient \(\alpha\) are not provided in the supplied excerpts. The papers do not say.

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: In H-Net, how does the routing module compute boundary probabilities $p_t$ and discrete boundary indicators $b_t$, and what is the formula and weight $\alpha$ for the auxiliary ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}$?
reply:
In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],
\]
with the convention \(p_1 = 1.0\) so that the sequence always starts with a boundary [hnet-C-013].

question: In Moshi's safety evaluation, why does AudioSeal signal-based watermarking fail when tested against Mimi, why does token-level generative watermarking also fail, and how does Moshi eliminate verbatim training-data regurgitation?
reply:
In Moshi’s safety evaluation, the signal‑based watermarking method AudioSeal fails when tested against the Mimi codec because the Mimi compression and decompression process discards the watermark. The Mimi codec is a low‑bit‑rate auto‑encoder that removes any information that is not directly needed for signal reconstruction, so the mark added by AudioSeal is reduced to a level where a water‑marked audio becomes indistinguishable from a non‑water‑marked one. This is reflected in Table 15, where the average detection score for the “Watermarked | Mimi compression & decompression” setting drops to 0.0805 for 10 s audio and 0.2404 for 1 min audio, compared with nearly perfect scores (≈ 1.0) when no compression is applied [moshi‑C‑075].

question: How does enabling Inner Monologue affect Moshi's spoken question answering accuracy across Web Questions, LlaMA-Questions, and Audio TriviaQA, and how can the same architecture be switched into streaming ASR or streaming TTS without changing the loss or architecture?
reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. The same multi‑stream architecture can be repurposed for streaming ASR or streaming TTS simply by adjusting the delay between text and audio tokens—no change to the loss function or the underlying model is required—because Inner Monologue’s prefix‑generation framework is compatible with any streaming inference setup [moshi-C-077].

The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions.  In a “flattened” sequence of length \(K\!\cdot\!S\) the model would need to make \(K\) times more predictions per time step, which quickly becomes prohibitive.  Instead, Moshi uses a large **Temporal Transformer** that processes a sequence of \(S\) time steps and produces a context vector \(z_s\).  A much smaller **Depth Transformer** then processes the \(K\) sub‑sequences (e.g., different audio codebooks or a text stream) conditioned on \(z_s\). model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

Moshi models **17 parallel token streams** (i.e., \(K=2Q+1\) with \(Q=8\)) at every 12.5 Hz timestep. These streams consist of one text stream for Moshi’s own speech, eight semantic‑audio streams for Moshi’s voice, and eight delayed acoustic streams for the other speaker (the “emphother”). model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?

This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax. question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

model_record.content:
Post‑Training Quantization (PTQ) applied to the Helium base model and to the final Moshi model (with a block size of 32) shows markedly different sensitivities to bit‑width reduction.  
For Helium, the MMLU scores remain close to the floating‑point baseline when the weights are quantized to 8 bits (W8A8) and even to 6 bits (W6A8). Only when the model is compressed to 4 bits (W4A8) does the score drop by about 2 points, and at 3 bits (W3A8) it falls to the mid‑40s, with a severe degradation at 2 bits (W2A8) to the mid‑20s. This reflects Helium’s robustness to aggressive weight quantization down to 4 bits (Table 10) [moshi-C-062].  

In contrast, the fully trained Moshi model is more sensitive. While a 6‑bit quantized Moshi (W6A8) stays within about 1 point of the floating‑point baseline, the performance deteriorates more sharply at 4 bits (W4A8), dropping to the mid‑40s, and plunges to the mid‑20s at 3 bits and 2 bits (W2A8) (Table 11) [moshi-C-063]. Thus, Moshi loses more linguistic capability than Helium when the weights are compressed to 4 bits or below.

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. question: How does enabling Inner Monologue affect Moshi's spoken question answering accuracy across Web Questions, LlaMA-Questions, and Audio TriviaQA, and how can the same architecture be switched into streaming ASR or streaming TTS without changing the loss or architecture?
reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. The same multi‑stream architecture can be repurposed for streaming ASR or streaming TTS simply by adjusting the delay between text and audio tokens—no change to the loss function or the underlying model is required—because Inner Monologue’s prefix‑generation framework is compatible with any streaming inference setup [moshi-C-077].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

The encoder is built from four residual convolutional blocks that alternate dilated and strided convolutions, followed by a final 1‑D strided convolution.  With striding factors (4, 5, 6, 8) and a final stride of 2, the network compresses the 24 kHz sample rate down to 12.5 latent timesteps per second, each timestep being a 512‑dimensional vector enc(x)∈ℝ¹²·⁵×⁵¹² [moshi‑C‑016]. question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5). Moshi models **17 parallel token streams** (i.e., \(K=2Q+1\) with \(Q=8\)) at every 12.5 Hz timestep. The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].
citations: Moshi v1, §3.3.2 Learning semantic-acoustic tokens with a split RVQ

The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

reply:
In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],
\]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does enabling Inner Monologue affect Moshi's spoken question answering accuracy across Web Questions, LlaMA-Questions, and Audio TriviaQA, and how can the same architecture be switched into streaming ASR or streaming TTS without changing the loss or architecture?
reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

Moshi models **17 parallel token streams** (i.e., \(K=2Q+1\) with \(Q=8\)) at every 12.5 Hz timestep. These streams consist of one text stream for Moshi’s own speech, eight semantic‑audio streams for Moshi’s voice, and eight delayed acoustic streams for the other speaker (the “emphother”). In total, at each timestep the model generates 17 tokens—16 for the two‑stream speech audio and one for Moshi’s text (or 17 when the inner‑monologue prefix is included) [moshi‑C‑028].

Moshi’s **theoretical latency** is **160 ms** (corresponding to a 12.5 Hz generation rate), and its **practical latency** measured in the paper is **200 ms** [moshi‑C‑001].

The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

Post‑Training Quantization (PTQ) applied to the Helium base model and to the final Moshi model (with a block size of 32) shows markedly different sensitivities to bit‑width reduction.  
For Helium, the MMLU scores remain close to the floating‑point baseline when the weights are quantized to 8 bits (W8A8) and even to 6 bits (W6A8). Only when the model is compressed to 4 bits (W4A8) does the score drop by about 2 points, and at 3 bits (W3A8) it falls to the mid‑40s, with a severe degradation at 2 bits (W2A8) to the mid‑20s. This reflects Helium’s robustness to aggressive weight quantization down to 4 bits (Table 10) [moshi-C-062].  

In contrast, the fully trained Moshi model is more sensitive. While a 6‑bit quantized Moshi (W6A8) stays within about 1 point of the floating‑point baseline, the performance deteriorates more sharply at 4 bits (W4A8), dropping to the mid‑40s, and plunges to the mid‑20s at 3 bits and 2 bits (W2A8) (Table 11) [moshi-C-063]. Thus, Moshi loses more linguistic capability than Helium when the weights are compressed to 4 bits or below.

model_record.content:
The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]  

The auxiliary ratio loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}\) is defined to enforce that the ratio of retained tokens matches a target ratio, but its explicit formula and the weighting coefficient \(\alpha\) are not provided in the supplied excerpts. The papers do not say.

The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions.  In a “flattened” sequence of length \(K\!\cdot\!S\) the model would need to make \(K\) times more predictions per time step, which quickly becomes prohibitive.  Instead, Moshi uses a large **Temporal Transformer** that processes a sequence of \(S\) time steps and produces a context vector \(z_s\).  A much smaller **Depth Transformer** then processes the \(K\) sub‑sequences (e.g., different audio codebooks or a text stream) conditioned on \(z_s\).  By scaling \(S\) for longer audio or increasing \(K\) for higher‑depth modeling, the architecture avoids the quadratic cost of a single flattened Transformer while still modeling the joint distribution across sub‑sequences [moshi-C-023][moshi-C-021].

question: Compare the tokenization approaches in all three papers, including vocabulary sizes, algorithms, and how each handles non-English languages or non-text modalities.
reply: In **hnet‑C‑064**, the discussion centers on *variable‑length* tokenization strategies for modalities beyond text. Two families of methods are highlighted: (1) latent‑space tokenization, where a learned autoencoder projects raw images, videos, or audio into a lower‑dimensional representation that is then discretized into tokens (e.g., Yu et al., 2024; Duggal et al., 2024), and (2) explicit token‑merging or “run‑length encoding” heuristics that merge adjacent tokens based on semantic or statistical criteria (e.g., Bolya et al., 2022; Choudhury et al., 2024). These methods can adapt token length to the information density of the input and are designed to work with non‑English text and multimodal data, but the paper does not give explicit vocabulary sizes; the token vocabularies are typically learned from the autoencoder’s bottleneck or from the discrete merging scheme and thus vary with the data modality [hnet‑C‑064].[Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions. model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

Moshi’s pre‑training stages use a cosine learning‑rate schedule starting at 3×10⁻⁴ (Helium) or 3×10⁻⁵ (Temporal Transformer) with a linear warm‑up, and the post‑training stage again uses a cosine schedule but with different initial rates for the two depth‑transformer branches [moshi‑C‑034].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],
\]

question: Compare the tokenization approaches in all three papers, including vocabulary sizes, algorithms, and how each handles non-English languages or non-text modalities.
reply: In **hnet‑C‑064**, the discussion centers on *variable‑length* tokenization strategies for modalities beyond text. Two families of methods are highlighted: (1) latent‑space tokenization, where a learned autoencoder projects raw images, videos, or audio into a lower‑dimensional representation that is then discretized into tokens (e.g., Yu et al., 2024; Duggal et al., 2024), and (2) explicit token‑merging or “run‑length encoding” heuristics that merge adjacent tokens based on semantic or statistical criteria (e.g., Bolya et al., 2022; Choudhury et al., 2024). These methods can adapt token length to the information density of the input and are designed to work with non‑English text and multimodal data, but the paper does not give explicit vocabulary sizes; the token vocabularies are typically learned from the autoencoder’s bottleneck or from the discrete merging scheme and thus vary with the data modality [hnet‑C‑064].[Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax. The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5). Among the three ablated components of the DC mechanism—smoothing module, cosine‑based routing, and STE—the **smoothing module** has the largest impact on training stability. The cosine routing and STE also contribute to stability and final performance, but their absence has a comparatively smaller effect than the loss of the smoothing module.

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

\[

\]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions.  In a “flattened” sequence of length \(K\!\cdot\!S\) the model would need to make \(K\) times more predictions per time step, which quickly becomes prohibitive. \[

\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

\[

\]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016].
