question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. reply: Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on all three benchmarks compared to a model trained without the method; for example, Moshi with Inner Monologue scores 26.6 % on Web Questions, 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA, whereas the same architecture without Inner Monologue achieves only 9.2 %, 21.0 %, and 7.3 % respectively (Table 8) [moshi-C-052]. question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: The Mimi codec first feeds a 24 kHz single‑channel waveform into a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder.  The encoder is built from four residual convolutional blocks that alternate dilated and strided convolutions, followed by a final 1‑D strided convolution.  With striding factors (4, 5, 6, 8) and a final stride of 2, the network compresses the 24 kHz sample rate down to 12.5 latent timesteps per second, each timestep being a 512‑dimensional vector enc(x)∈ℝ¹²·⁵×⁵¹² [moshi‑C‑016]. question: Compare the tokenization approaches in all three papers, including vocabulary sizes, algorithms, and how each handles non-English languages or non-text modalities.

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

reply:
In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]
A discrete boundary indicator is produced by thresholding this probability:
\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax.  The dechunking layer then upsamples the smoothed representations with a confidence‑weighted Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) that preserves gradient flow while still enforcing discrete‑like behaviour in the forward pass [hnet‑C‑014], [hnet‑C‑015].[Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

Token‑level generative watermarking also fails because the token representation produced by Moshi’s discrete latent space is not idempotent. This lack of stability makes the hash‑based sampling bias unreliable for detection. Moreover, the tokens are sensitive to moderate temporal shifts and the dependency on previous quantizer levels further reduces robustness, as quantified in Table 16. In H‑Net, the routing module first projects each encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) using learnable linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to obtain query‑ and key‑vectors:
\[
\mathbf{q}_t = W_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad \mathbf{k}_t = W_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]
The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent projections:
\[
p_t \;=\; \frac12\!\left(1 \;-\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}{\lVert\mathbf{q}_t\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\rVert}\right) \;\in [0,1].
\]

\[
b_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[p_t \ge 0.5\bigr],

The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions.  In a “flattened” sequence of length \(K\!\cdot\!S\) the model would need to make \(K\) times more predictions per time step, which quickly becomes prohibitive.  Instead, Moshi uses a large **Temporal Transformer** that processes a sequence of \(S\) time steps and produces a context vector \(z_s\).  A much smaller **Depth Transformer** then processes the \(K\) sub‑sequences (e.g., different audio codebooks or a text stream) conditioned on \(z_s\).  By scaling \(S\) for longer audio or increasing \(K\) for higher‑depth modeling, the architecture avoids the quadratic cost of a single flattened Transformer while still modeling the joint distribution across sub‑sequences [moshi-C-023][moshi-C-021].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5). question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: Compare the tokenization approaches in all three papers, including vocabulary sizes, algorithms, and how each handles non-English languages or non-text modalities.
reply: In **hnet‑C‑064**, the discussion centers on *variable‑length* tokenization strategies for modalities beyond text. Two families of methods are highlighted: (1) latent‑space tokenization, where a learned autoencoder projects raw images, videos, or audio into a lower‑dimensional representation that is then discretized into tokens (e.g., Yu et al., 2024; Duggal et al., 2024), and (2) explicit token‑merging or “run‑length encoding” heuristics that merge adjacent tokens based on semantic or statistical criteria (e.g., Bolya et al., 2022; Choudhury et al., 2024). model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].
citations: Moshi v1, §3.3.2 Learning semantic-acoustic tokens with a split RVQ

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax.  The dechunking layer then upsamples the smoothed representations with a confidence‑weighted Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) that preserves gradient flow while still enforcing discrete‑like behaviour in the forward pass [hnet‑C‑014], [hnet‑C‑015].[Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]

H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax.  The dechunking layer then upsamples the smoothed representations with a confidence‑weighted Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) that preserves gradient flow while still enforcing discrete‑like behaviour in the forward pass [hnet‑C‑014], [hnet‑C‑015].

Among the three ablated components of the DC mechanism—smoothing module, cosine‑based routing, and STE—the **smoothing module** has the largest impact on training stability.  Ablation studies show that removing the smoothing module (“w/o smoothing”) causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios throughout training and leads to substantial performance degradation, indicating that smooth gradient flow through the decompression process is critical for stable end‑to‑end learning [hnet‑C‑042].  The cosine routing and STE also contribute to stability and final performance, but their absence has a comparatively smaller effect than the loss of the smoothing module.

The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[

\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

\[

\]

\[

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

Token‑level generative watermarking also fails because the token representation produced by Moshi’s discrete latent space is not idempotent. When a waveform is generated from tokens and then re‑encoded back into tokens, the resulting token sequence differs from the original, even if no external noise is added. This lack of stability makes the hash‑based sampling bias unreliable for detection. Moreover, the tokens are sensitive to moderate temporal shifts and the dependency on previous quantizer levels further reduces robustness, as quantified in Table 16. These issues prevent a robust watermark detector from working, leading to failure of the generative watermarking approach [moshi‑C‑073], [moshi‑C‑074].

reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5). Among the three ablated components of the DC mechanism—smoothing module, cosine‑based routing, and STE—the **smoothing module** has the largest impact on training stability. The cosine routing and STE also contribute to stability and final performance, but their absence has a comparatively smaller effect than the loss of the smoothing module.

model_record.content:
The Moshi v1 paper tackles sequence‑length scaling by introducing a *hierarchical* autoregressive model—the RQ‑Transformer—where a large Temporal Transformer first processes long‑time‑step sequences to produce a context vector, and a smaller Depth Transformer then predicts the tokens within each time step. This two‑stage design allows the model to scale to longer sequences simply by increasing the number of time steps \(S\), while keeping the per‑step depth \(K\) small, thereby reducing the overall computational burden per prediction step [moshi-C-023][moshi-C-021].  

In the H‑Net v2 discussion, the authors argue that the traditional tokenization step is a major source of computational waste because it forces models to handle very long discrete token streams. They propose *tokenizer‑free* or *data‑dependent chunking* strategies (e.g., run‑length encoding, entropy‑based delimiters, and auto‑encoder latent space tokenization) that collapse raw inputs into far fewer, information‑dense tokens. By doing so, they reduce both sequence length and the cost of self‑attention, thereby addressing the computational bottleneck inherent to autoregressive or transduction models [hnet-C-002][hnet-C-064].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?
reply: H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax. model_record.content:
The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]

model_record.content:
The routing module computes boundary probabilities and discrete boundary indicators as follows: it first projects adjacent encoder outputs \(\hat x_{t-1}\) and \(\hat x_t\) with learned linear maps \(W_q\) and \(W_k\), then evaluates the cosine similarity between the projected vectors. The resulting similarity is transformed into a boundary probability by

\[
p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{|q_t||k_{t-1}|}\right)\quad\in[0,1]
\]

and a discrete boundary indicator is obtained by thresholding this probability at 0.5:

\[
b_t = \mathbb{1}_{p_t\ge 0.5}\,,
\]

with \(p_1\) fixed to 1.0 to ensure a boundary at the sequence start. [hnet-C-013]  

The auxiliary ratio loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}\) is defined to enforce that the ratio of retained tokens matches a target ratio, but its explicit formula and the weighting coefficient \(\alpha\) are not provided in the supplied excerpts. The papers do not say.

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

This lack of stability makes the hash‑based sampling bias unreliable for detection. Moreover, the tokens are sensitive to moderate temporal shifts and the dependency on previous quantizer levels further reduces robustness, as quantified in Table 16. question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

The RQ‑Transformer architecture in Moshi v1 tackles the sequence‑length problem by explicitly separating the temporal and depth dimensions.  In a “flattened” sequence of length \(K\!\cdot\!S\) the model would need to make \(K\) times more predictions per time step, which quickly becomes prohibitive. H‑Net renders the inherently discrete operations of dynamic chunking and decompression differentiable by inserting a **smoothing module** that replaces hard boundary decisions with a smooth exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) interpolation.  The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5).  This transforms the discrete up‑sampling boundary into a continuous operation, allowing gradients to flow through the boundary probabilities \(P_t\) without resorting to stochastic tricks such as Gumbel‑Softmax.  The dechunking layer then upsamples the smoothed representations with a confidence‑weighted Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) that preserves gradient flow while still enforcing discrete‑like behaviour in the forward pass [hnet‑C‑014], [hnet‑C‑015].

Among the three ablated components of the DC mechanism—smoothing module, cosine‑based routing, and STE—the **smoothing module** has the largest impact on training stability.  Ablation studies show that removing the smoothing module (“w/o smoothing”) causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios throughout training and leads to substantial performance degradation, indicating that smooth gradient flow through the decompression process is critical for stable end‑to‑end learning [hnet‑C‑042].  The cosine routing and STE also contribute to stability and final performance, but their absence has a comparatively smaller effect than the loss of the smoothing module.

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
reply: Mimi first encodes a 24 kHz waveform with a causal SeaNet‑style autoencoder that uses four residual convolutional blocks (striding factors 4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1D convolution of stride 2, projecting the raw audio to a latent sequence of 12.5 steps per second with a 512‑dimensional vector, which gives a bitrate of 1.1 kbps when compressed with a Residual Vector Quantizer [moshi-C-016]. To keep semantic information separate from acoustic detail, Mimi replaces a single 8‑level RVQ with a split RVQ: it first distills phonetic (semantic) features into a plain vector quantizer using WavLM embeddings, and then applies a parallel 7‑level RVQ to the residual, summing both outputs; this avoids forcing the first quantizer to trade audio quality for phonetic discriminability and yields a better semantic‑acoustic trade‑off [moshi-C-019].

model_record.content: H-Net makes discrete chunking differentiable by inserting a smoothing module that replaces hard chunk boundaries with an exponential moving average, thereby turning the discrete upsampling operation into a continuous, differentiable computation that allows gradients to flow through boundary decisions [hnet-C-014]. It further introduces a straight‑through estimator (STE) in the upsampler that rounds confidence scores to 1.0 during the forward pass while preserving continuous gradients during back‑propagation, and it weights the decompression step by confidence scores so that confident boundary predictions receive direct gradient feedback [hnet-C-015]. Among the three ablated dynamic‑chunking components, the smoothing module has the largest impact on training stability; removing it causes severe fluctuations in compression ratios and prevents the model from learning consistent chunk‑boundary patterns, leading to substantial performance degradation [hnet-C-042].

question: How does H-Net make discrete chunking and decompression differentiable during training, and which of the three ablated DC components (smoothing module, cosine routing, or STE) has the largest impact on training stability?

The module computes a smoothed representation \(\bar z_t\) from the current chunk \(z_t\) and the previous smoothed value \(\bar z_{t-1}\) using the EMA formula \( \bar z_t = P_t \, z_t + (1-P_t)\,\bar z_{t-1}\) (Eq. 5). The encoder projects a single-channel waveform xinR^L to a latent representation enc(x)inR^Stimes D by cascading residual convolutional blocks that interleave dilated ( van den Oord et al., 2016 ) and strided convolutions along with ELU ( Clevert et al., 2016 ) non-linearities and Weight Normalization ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) . All convolutions are causal, such that this autoencoder can run in a streaming fashion. With 4 convolutional blocks and respective striding factors (4,5,6,8) , and a final 1D convolution with stride 2, Mimi’s encoder projects a 24kHz waveform to a latent representation of 12.5 frames per second and dimension D=512 . Symmetrically, the decoder adopts a similar structure but with transposed convolutions rather than strided ones, to project the latent representation back to 24kHz audio. We discretize the latent space with a Residual Vector Quantizer ( Zeghidour et al., 2022 ) , which iteratively applies vector quantization (VQ) to the residuals of the previous quantizer. With Q quantizers, each with a codebook of N_A centroids, the RVQ discretizes the latent space into 1,dots,N_A^Stimes Q . [Attention v7, §5.4 Regularization]
Attention v7 > §5 Training > 5.4 Regularization
We employ three types of regularization during training:

Residual Dropout

We apply dropout [ 33 ] to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized. In addition, we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks. For the base model, we use a rate of P_drop=0.1 .

Label Smoothing

During training, we employed label smoothing of value epsilon_ls=0.1 [ 36 ] . This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

This corresponds to increasing the learning rate linearly for the first warmup_steps training steps, and decreasing it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. We used warmup_steps=4000 .

Enabling Inner Monologue dramatically improves Moshi’s spoken‑question‑answering accuracy.  Compared with the same model trained without Inner Monologue, Moshi’s accuracy rises from 9.2 % to 26.6 % on Web Questions, from 21.0 % to 62.3 % on LlaMA‑Questions, and from 7.3 % to 22.8 % on Audio TriviaQA—roughly a three‑fold increase on each benchmark.  This large jump demonstrates that prefixing audio tokens with text tokens (the Inner Monologue) is essential for the model’s performance in spoken question answering [moshi-C-053][moshi-C-052].

Because Inner Monologue only changes the ordering of text and audio tokens, the same multi‑stream architecture can be re‑used for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) or streaming text‑to‑speech (TTS) by simply altering the delay between the two token streams.  The loss functions and model structure remain unchanged; only the temporal alignment between the textual and acoustic outputs is shifted, enabling the system to operate either as an ASR or a TTS system [moshi-C-077].

These findings align with recent research demonstrating SSMs’ advantages over Transformers for fine-grained sequence modeling ( Goel et al., 2022 ; Caduceus ) , as corroborated by MambaByte’s superior performance over LlamaByte in Figure 3 . A natural question arises: does the importance of Mamba layers (i) stem specifically from processing fine-grained byte inputs , or (ii) because they are better for compressing information into the next stage, even at coarser input resolutions ? To investigate these hypotheses, we train a 1-stage H-Net on top of BPE-tokenized inputs processed by the GPT-2 tokenizer. We then evaluate six different encoder-decoder combinations. • If hypothesis (i) holds, then we would expect different combinations of Mamba/Transformer layers in the encoder/decoder to have similar performance, since it is known that they have similar performance on standard tokenized language modeling. • If hypothesis (ii) holds, then we would expect that encoders/decoders using some Mamba layers to be better than pure Transformer layers. As demonstrated in Figure 10 , Mamba layers prove significantly important even when processing BPE tokens rather than raw bytes, providing evidence for the second hypothesis. We hypothesize that this consistent advantage across input granularities stems from fundamental architectural differences between SSMs and Transformers. While Transformers naturally store complete key-value caches for all positions, SSMs are designed to compress information into fixed-size states. This compression-oriented architecture aligns naturally with our chunking mechanism, which requires aggregating multiple input vectors into consolidated representations. The inherent compression capability of Mamba layers makes them particularly well-suited for the encoder and decoder roles in our hierarchical architecture ( Gu, 2025 ) . Based on these findings, we employ Mamba layers throughout all encoders and decoders in our final H-Net configuration, as detailed in Table 1 . These findings transfer to more general hierarchical structures (such as a 2-stage H-Net at the byte level), in which case the outermost encoder and decoder layers ( E^0 and D^0 ) serve a similar role as the GPT-2 tokenizer and the inner layers ( E^1 and D^1 ) would share similar findings of benefiting from using Mamba layers. To this end, we compared H-Net (2-stage) with an identical model where we replaced the Transformer stack with a hybrid model containing both 20 Mamba-2 and 7 Transformer layers interleaved in a 3:1 ratio. Hybrid architectures have shown promise in isotropic (BPE) models ( Waleffe et al., 2024 ) , and similarly perform better for our choice of main network ( Figure 11 ). Encoder and Decoder Networks. The encoder and decoder networks in H-Net face unique design constraints due to their dual objectives and computational requirements. Each encoder must simultaneously (i) preserve fine-grained information for transmission to its corresponding decoder through residual connections ( 3 ), and (ii) compress inputs into chunks of richer representations for the main network. The decoder, in turn, must effectively combine coarse-grained representations from the main network with fine-grained details from the encoder residuals. Importantly, both encoders and decoders operate on uncompressed sequences, making computational efficiency a significant design constraint that shapes our architectural choices. Recent studies demonstrate that state space models (SSMs) ( Gu et al., 2022 ; Mamba ) excel at processing fine-grained data including audio ( Goel et al., 2022 ) , DNA sequences ( Caduceus ) , and robotic control signals ( Lu et al., 2023 ) . Based on these insights, we employ Mamba-2 layers ( Dao & Gu, 2024 ) as the primary building blocks for the encoder and decoder networks. This choice yields two significant benefits: effective handling of fine-grained inputs, and substantially improved efficiency when processing long, uncompressed sequences. Our ablation studies ( Section 3.3 ) confirm that SSM-based encoders/decoders significantly outperform Transformer layers, not just at the byte level but even on coarser inputs, which we attribute to their stronger inductive bias for compression which helps build abstractions ( Gu, 2025 ) . Main Network. H-Net’s computational efficiency stems from strategic parameter allocation. We concentrate the majority of model capacity in the main network, which operates on progressively compressed sequences. After S stages of compression, the main network receives sequences where L^Sll L^0 , enabling much larger networks within the same computational budget. This design reflects two key principles: (i) compressed sequences allow more parameters and compute per chunk, and (ii) higher-level abstractions benefit from increased processing power. The main network functions as a standard language model and can employ any sequence mixing architecture. We default to Transformer layers for two reasons: compressed representations align well with Transformers’ strengths in processing discrete, semantically-rich tokens, and this choice enables more controlled comparison with traditional BPE-based Transformer baselines in our experiments. However, the modular design also allows straightforward substitution with alternative architectures ( e.g., a state space model, hybrid, or H-Net itself) as explored in our ablations. [Moshi v1, §0 Abstract]
Moshi v1 > §0 Abstract
We introduce Moshi, a speech-text foundation model and full-duplex spoken dialogue framework. Current systems for spoken dialogue rely on pipelines of independent components, namely voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue and text-to-speech. Such frameworks cannot emulate the experience of real conversations. First, their complexity induces a latency of several seconds between interactions. Second, text being the intermediate modality for dialogue, non-linguistic information that modifies meaning— such as emotion or non-speech sounds— is lost in the interaction. Finally, they rely on a segmentation into speaker turns, which does not take into account overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections. Moshi solves these independent issues altogether by casting spoken dialogue as speech-to-speech generation. Starting from a text language model backbone, Moshi generates speech as tokens from the residual quantizer of a neural audio codec, while modeling separately its own speech and that of the user into parallel streams. This allows for the removal of explicit speaker turns, and the modeling of arbitrary conversational dynamics. We moreover extend the hierarchical semantic-to-acoustic token generation of previous work to first predict time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens. Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech. Our resulting model is the first real-time full-duplex spoken large language model, with a theoretical latency of 160ms, 200ms in practice, and is available at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi .

[Moshi v1, §5.5 Spoken question answering]
Moshi v1 > §5 Evaluation > 5.5 Spoken question answering
Metrics.

We evaluate the spoken question answering abilities of our final multi-stream Moshi model. We rely on Spoken Web Questions and Llama Questions, both introduced by Nachmani et al. (2024) . We also synthesize an audio version of TriviaQA as another benchmark. When evaluating Moshi, we insert the audio tokens of the question into the user stream to simulate a user interaction.

Baselines.

We compare to Spectron and baselines used by Nachmani et al. (2024) , all having been already introduced in Section 5.4 except for SpeechGPT ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) . As a way to measure the impact of Inner Monologue on spoken fluency, we compare these baselines with Moshi trained with and without Inner Monologue. Moreover, to quantify an eventual degradation in knowledge due to training on audio data, we also compare to Helium when evaluated on the textual counterpart to each spoken dataset.

Results.

Table 8 reports accuracies on the three benchmarks. The most striking result is the impact of Inner Monologue on Moshi’s performance, almost tripling its accuracy on all benchmarks, and significantly improving over previous work. This is remarkable as Inner Monologue only marginally increases inference cost (each multi-stream timestep requires generating 17 tokens, instead of 16 without Inner Monologue). We emphasize again that among all models in this comparison, Moshi not only provides the best spoken question answering performance, but is also the only one to model jointly semantic and acoustic tokens, such that it can handle interactions between arbitrary voices in many conditions.

Discussion.

Despite the strong performance of Moshi, we observe a weaker performance than its original Helium checkpoint, which is consistent with the reduced MMLU of 49.7 reported in Table 7 from 54.3 with Helium. While the moderate differences on Web Questions and Llama Questions can be explained by training on audio data and thus reducing the amount of parameters dedicated to textual knowledge, the very large difference on Trivia QA incites us to inspect more thoroughly patterns of errors. We find in particular that multiple-sentence questions (e.g. “The Terror of the Monster was an early title for a best-selling novel which inspired one of the highest-grossing movies of the mid-70’s. Under what name did it eventually terrify the reading and film going public?”) or ones with specific syntactic structure (e.g. “On the human body, a keloid is a type of what?”) are particularly challenging for Moshi, due to it being finetuned on oral-style conversations that do not display such patterns. We thus hypothesize that covering more syntactic scenarios during finetuning could reduce this gap.

[Moshi v1, §7 Conclusion]
Moshi v1 > §7 Conclusion
In this work, we introduce Moshi, the first real-time, full-duplex spoken dialogue system. The first component of Moshi is Helium, a 7B parameter text LLM which is competitive with open-weights models trained with a similar compute budget. To encode audio into discrete units amenable to language modeling, we introduce Mimi, a semantic-acoustic neural audio codec which provides state-of-the-art audio quality at low bitrates while operating at low framerates compatible with real-time generation. We then introduce a new, hierarchical multi-stream architecture that supports generating arbitrary conversations in a speech-to-speech manner. We moreover show that speech-to-speech generation can be drastically improved by Inner Monologue, a new method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, while remaining compatible with streaming inference. Our experiments show that Moshi demonstrates state-of-the-art spoken question answering and dialogue modeling while displaying satisfying levels of safety by not generating toxic content and remaining consistent in its voice. To summarize, we introduce a complete suite of models and recipes, from text LLMs to neural audio codecs and generative audio models, which we combine into a real-time spoken dialogue system with a 160ms theoretical latency able to follow complex multi-turn conversations across 5 minutes. We release both Mimi and Moshi to foster the development of such applications. Additionally, we show how our Inner Monologue method allows designing streaming TTS and streaming ASR just by changing the delay between text and audio tokens. We believe that both Inner Monologue and multi-stream modeling will have a positive impact on speech-to-speech and audio-to-audio beyond dialogue modeling.

H-Net v2 > §3 Experiments > 3.3 Ablation Studies
For ablation studies, we employ H-Net at Large scale following the configurations in Table 1 , training on 36 B tokens randomly sampled from FineWeb-Edu. Importance of Components in H-Net. Figure 7 illustrates the impact of each architectural component on both model performance and compression ratio ( L^s+1/L^s ) stability during training. We conduct three targeted ablations: (i) using direct upsampling tildez_t=hatz_t by removing the smoothing module ( w/o smoothing ), (ii) replacing the routing module that is based on scaled cosine similarity, with direct probability prediction from individual inputs ( w/o cosine routing ), and (iii) skipping the straight-through estimator in equation ( 9 ) (w/o STE). The smoothing module proves essential for stable training dynamics. Without this module, compression ratios fluctuate severely throughout training, preventing the model from learning consistent chunking boundaries. This instability directly manifests as substantial performance degradation, confirming that smooth gradient flow through the decompression process is crucial for effective end-to-end learning. While less critical than the smoothing module, both the similarity-based routing module and STE operation exhibit importance in training stability and final performance. These components help maintain consistent compression ratios and lead to more interpretable chunking patterns. The similarity-based approach particularly enables the model to identify natural linguistic boundaries ( e.g., whitespaces, subwords) by comparing adjacent representations rather than making isolated predictions. Encoder & Decoder Layer Selection. The composition of sequence mixing layers in H-Net’s encoders and decoders substantially influences both compression efficiency and modeling capability. We systematically evaluate different architectural combinations using H-Net (1-stage) while fixing all other configurations in Table 1 the same. Four distinct encoder-decoder ( E^0 - D^0 ) pairings are tested: M4-M4, M2T1-T1M2, T1M2-M2T1, and T2-T2, where M denotes a Mamba-2 layer and T denotes a Transformer layer. These combinations are chosen by keeping the symmetry and replacing each Transformer layer with two Mamba-2 layers, as they contain equivalent parameter counts — 12D^2 for Transformer ( 4D^2 for the attention mechanism and 8D^2 for an MLP) vs. approx 6D^2 per Mamba-2 layer (no MLP). Figure 8 and Figure 9 demonstrate that Mamba layers are essential for effective byte-level sequence processing. For both H-Net and SpaceByte++, the pure Transformer configuration (T2-T2) exhibits by far the worst performance despite using more FLOPs (it also down-compresses sequences poorly compared to other configurations, thus using more compute in the main network). This configuration struggles to compress byte sequences effectively, resulting in both computational waste and degraded modeling performance. Performance improves monotonically with increased Mamba layer allocation, achieving optimal results with the highest compression efficiency in the pure Mamba configuration (M4-M4). These findings align with recent research demonstrating SSMs’ advantages over Transformers for fine-grained sequence modeling ( Goel et al., 2022 ; Caduceus )

[Attention v7, §3.1 Encoder and Decoder Stacks]
Attention v7 > §3 Model Architecture > 3.1 Encoder and Decoder Stacks
Encoder:

The encoder is composed of a stack of N=6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [ 11 ] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [ 1 ] . That is, the output of each sub-layer is LayerNorm(x+Sublayer(x)) , where Sublayer(x) is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension d_model=512 .

Decoder:

The decoder is also composed of a stack of N=6 identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i .

[Moshi v1, §0 Abstract]
Moshi v1 > §0 Abstract
We introduce Moshi, a speech-text foundation model and full-duplex spoken dialogue framework. Current systems for spoken dialogue rely on pipelines of independent components, namely voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue and text-to-speech. Such frameworks cannot emulate the experience of real conversations. First, their complexity induces a latency of several seconds between interactions. Second, text being the intermediate modality for dialogue, non-linguistic information that modifies meaning— such as emotion or non-speech sounds— is lost in the interaction. Finally, they rely on a segmentation into speaker turns, which does not take into account overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections. Moshi solves these independent issues altogether by casting spoken dialogue as speech-to-speech generation. Starting from a text language model backbone, Moshi generates speech as tokens from the residual quantizer of a neural audio codec, while modeling separately its own speech and that of the user into parallel streams. This allows for the removal of explicit speaker turns, and the modeling of arbitrary conversational dynamics. We moreover extend the hierarchical semantic-to-acoustic token generation of previous work to first predict time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens. Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech. Our resulting model is the first real-time full-duplex spoken large language model, with a theoretical latency of 160ms, 200ms in practice, and is available at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi .

We first compute the Shannon entropy H across windows of fixed size C at each timestep i for each of this stream independently. This yields H^0_i=H(W_[i-C:i]) for text, and H^k_i=H(A_[i-C:i],k) for audio. Note that we only consider the stream of Moshi ( kleq Q ). We use C=64 in practice, which corresponds to roughly 4.5 seconds of audio once decoded, and ignore all the leading C tokens as they have a shorted context (and include the prompt used for generation). We observe qualitatively that the entropy spectrum is often indicative of artifacts or degradations of the audio samples. Formally we define three types of artifacts from the entropy statistics, as described below. In practice, we characterize the presence or absence of each artifact over non-overlapping windows of omega=64 tokens, as illustrated in Figure 10 . Repetitive text A first observed degradation is the model quickly repeating short sentences or words. This characterized by the text entropy being almost flat over a window H^0_i:i+omega , but non zero (as more than one token is repeated), as seen in Figure 10 (c) . We measure the “flatness” of H^0_i:i+omega by fitting a linear regression model to it and verifying whether the slope is below a certain threshold hyperparameter eta_flat=1e-3 . Routing Module.

In natural data, meaningful boundaries tend to emerge at points of contextual or semantic shift. From this observation, we add an inductive bias by measuring the similarity between adjacent representations: when context changes, consecutive vectors should exhibit lower similarity. The routing module implements this intuition through cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs. The downsampler compresses encoder outputs hatx^s into a reduced set of vectors x^s+1 using boundary indicators b_t^s_t=1^L^s . Among potential compression strategies – including mean pooling, max pooling, or cross-attention – we adopt direct selection of boundary-marked vectors for its simplicity and effectiveness (see Section E.1 for ablations).

As illustrated in Figure 1 -(b), this approach follows a straightforward selection rule: vectors where b_t=1 are retained in the compressed sequence x^s+1 , while those where b_t=0 are discarded. [Moshi v1, §5.5 Spoken question answering]
Moshi v1 > §5 Evaluation > 5.5 Spoken question answering
Metrics.

We evaluate the spoken question answering abilities of our final multi-stream Moshi model. We rely on Spoken Web Questions and Llama Questions, both introduced by Nachmani et al. (2024) . We also synthesize an audio version of TriviaQA as another benchmark. When evaluating Moshi, we insert the audio tokens of the question into the user stream to simulate a user interaction.

Baselines.

We compare to Spectron and baselines used by Nachmani et al. (2024) , all having been already introduced in Section 5.4 except for SpeechGPT ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) . As a way to measure the impact of Inner Monologue on spoken fluency, we compare these baselines with Moshi trained with and without Inner Monologue. Moreover, to quantify an eventual degradation in knowledge due to training on audio data, we also compare to Helium when evaluated on the textual counterpart to each spoken dataset.

Results.

Table 8 reports accuracies on the three benchmarks. The most striking result is the impact of Inner Monologue on Moshi’s performance, almost tripling its accuracy on all benchmarks, and significantly improving over previous work. This is remarkable as Inner Monologue only marginally increases inference cost (each multi-stream timestep requires generating 17 tokens, instead of 16 without Inner Monologue). We emphasize again that among all models in this comparison, Moshi not only provides the best spoken question answering performance, but is also the only one to model jointly semantic and acoustic tokens, such that it can handle interactions between arbitrary voices in many conditions.

Discussion.

Despite the strong performance of Moshi, we observe a weaker performance than its original Helium checkpoint, which is consistent with the reduced MMLU of 49.7 reported in Table 7 from 54.3 with Helium. While the moderate differences on Web Questions and Llama Questions can be explained by training on audio data and thus reducing the amount of parameters dedicated to textual knowledge, the very large difference on Trivia QA incites us to inspect more thoroughly patterns of errors. We find in particular that multiple-sentence questions (e.g. “The Terror of the Monster was an early title for a best-selling novel which inspired one of the highest-grossing movies of the mid-70’s. Under what name did it eventually terrify the reading and film going public?”) or ones with specific syntactic structure (e.g. “On the human body, a keloid is a type of what?”) are particularly challenging for Moshi, due to it being finetuned on oral-style conversations that do not display such patterns. We thus hypothesize that covering more syntactic scenarios during finetuning could reduce this gap.

[Moshi v1, §7 Conclusion]
Moshi v1 > §7 Conclusion
In this work, we introduce Moshi, the first real-time, full-duplex spoken dialogue system. The first component of Moshi is Helium, a 7B parameter text LLM which is competitive with open-weights models trained with a similar compute budget. To encode audio into discrete units amenable to language modeling, we introduce Mimi, a semantic-acoustic neural audio codec which provides state-of-the-art audio quality at low bitrates while operating at low framerates compatible with real-time generation. We then introduce a new, hierarchical multi-stream architecture that supports generating arbitrary conversations in a speech-to-speech manner. We moreover show that speech-to-speech generation can be drastically improved by Inner Monologue, a new method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, while remaining compatible with streaming inference. Our experiments show that Moshi demonstrates state-of-the-art spoken question answering and dialogue modeling while displaying satisfying levels of safety by not generating toxic content and remaining consistent in its voice. To summarize, we introduce a complete suite of models and recipes, from text LLMs to neural audio codecs and generative audio models, which we combine into a real-time spoken dialogue system with a 160ms theoretical latency able to follow complex multi-turn conversations across 5 minutes. We release both Mimi and Moshi to foster the development of such applications. Additionally, we show how our Inner Monologue method allows designing streaming TTS and streaming ASR just by changing the delay between text and audio tokens. We believe that both Inner Monologue and multi-stream modeling will have a positive impact on speech-to-speech and audio-to-audio beyond dialogue modeling.

The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to counteract the effect that, for large values of the key dimension \(d_k\), the dot products between query and key vectors tend to grow in magnitude. When the components of the query and key vectors are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Large variances push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, hurting learning. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the dot‑product distribution so that its variance is roughly 1, keeping the softmax in a numerically stable regime. [attention‑C-008]

[Moshi v1, §0 Abstract]
Moshi v1 > §0 Abstract
We introduce Moshi, a speech-text foundation model and full-duplex spoken dialogue framework. Current systems for spoken dialogue rely on pipelines of independent components, namely voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue and text-to-speech. Such frameworks cannot emulate the experience of real conversations. First, their complexity induces a latency of several seconds between interactions. Second, text being the intermediate modality for dialogue, non-linguistic information that modifies meaning— such as emotion or non-speech sounds— is lost in the interaction. Finally, they rely on a segmentation into speaker turns, which does not take into account overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections. Moshi solves these independent issues altogether by casting spoken dialogue as speech-to-speech generation. Starting from a text language model backbone, Moshi generates speech as tokens from the residual quantizer of a neural audio codec, while modeling separately its own speech and that of the user into parallel streams. This allows for the removal of explicit speaker turns, and the modeling of arbitrary conversational dynamics. We moreover extend the hierarchical semantic-to-acoustic token generation of previous work to first predict time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens. Not only this “Inner Monologue” method significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech, but we also illustrate how it can provide streaming speech recognition and text-to-speech. Our resulting model is the first real-time full-duplex spoken large language model, with a theoretical latency of 160ms, 200ms in practice, and is available at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi .

These findings align with recent research demonstrating SSMs’ advantages over Transformers for fine-grained sequence modeling ( Goel et al., 2022 ; Caduceus ) , as corroborated by MambaByte’s superior performance over LlamaByte in Figure 3 . A natural question arises: does the importance of Mamba layers (i) stem specifically from processing fine-grained byte inputs , or (ii) because they are better for compressing information into the next stage, even at coarser input resolutions ? To investigate these hypotheses, we train a 1-stage H-Net on top of BPE-tokenized inputs processed by the GPT-2 tokenizer. We then evaluate six different encoder-decoder combinations. • If hypothesis (i) holds, then we would expect different combinations of Mamba/Transformer layers in the encoder/decoder to have similar performance, since it is known that they have similar performance on standard tokenized language modeling. • If hypothesis (ii) holds, then we would expect that encoders/decoders using some Mamba layers to be better than pure Transformer layers. As demonstrated in Figure 10 , Mamba layers prove significantly important even when processing BPE tokens rather than raw bytes, providing evidence for the second hypothesis. We hypothesize that this consistent advantage across input granularities stems from fundamental architectural differences between SSMs and Transformers. While Transformers naturally store complete key-value caches for all positions, SSMs are designed to compress information into fixed-size states. This compression-oriented architecture aligns naturally with our chunking mechanism, which requires aggregating multiple input vectors into consolidated representations. The inherent compression capability of Mamba layers makes them particularly well-suited for the encoder and decoder roles in our hierarchical architecture ( Gu, 2025 ) . Based on these findings, we employ Mamba layers throughout all encoders and decoders in our final H-Net configuration, as detailed in Table 1 . These findings transfer to more general hierarchical structures (such as a 2-stage H-Net at the byte level), in which case the outermost encoder and decoder layers ( E^0 and D^0 ) serve a similar role as the GPT-2 tokenizer and the inner layers ( E^1 and D^1 ) would share similar findings of benefiting from using Mamba layers. To this end, we compared H-Net (2-stage) with an identical model where we replaced the Transformer stack with a hybrid model containing both 20 Mamba-2 and 7 Transformer layers interleaved in a 3:1 ratio. Each encoder must simultaneously (i) preserve fine-grained information for transmission to its corresponding decoder through residual connections ( 3 ), and (ii) compress inputs into chunks of richer representations for the main network. The decoder, in turn, must effectively combine coarse-grained representations from the main network with fine-grained details from the encoder residuals. Importantly, both encoders and decoders operate on uncompressed sequences, making computational efficiency a significant design constraint that shapes our architectural choices. Recent studies demonstrate that state space models (SSMs) ( Gu et al., 2022 ; Mamba ) excel at processing fine-grained data including audio ( Goel et al., 2022 ) , DNA sequences ( Caduceus ) , and robotic control signals ( Lu et al., 2023 ) . Based on these insights, we employ Mamba-2 layers ( Dao & Gu, 2024 ) as the primary building blocks for the encoder and decoder networks. This choice yields two significant benefits: effective handling of fine-grained inputs, and substantially improved efficiency when processing long, uncompressed sequences. Our ablation studies ( Section 3.3 ) confirm that SSM-based encoders/decoders significantly outperform Transformer layers, not just at the byte level but even on coarser inputs, which we attribute to their stronger inductive bias for compression which helps build abstractions ( Gu, 2025 ) . We concentrate the majority of model capacity in the main network, which operates on progressively compressed sequences. We default to Transformer layers for two reasons: compressed representations align well with Transformers’ strengths in processing discrete, semantically-rich tokens, and this choice enables more controlled comparison with traditional BPE-based Transformer baselines in our experiments.
